entries.title: ‘Delights await!’: Margaret Atwood and other writers on Nobel winner Anne Carson
entries.summary: The Handmaid’s Tale author is joined by Emily Wilson, Ocean Vuong and Booker-shortlisted writer Rebecca Perry in celebrating the newly announced Nobel laureateAnne Carson wins Nobel prize in literature 2026Where to start with: Anne CarsonAnne Carson’s work has long been admired among poets of many countries. For new readers, I would recommend The Beauty of the Husband – direct and visceral, funny
entries.content:
Margaret Atwood

Anne Carson’s work has long been admired among poets of many countries. For new readers, I would recommend The Beauty of the Husband – direct and visceral, funny and angry and sad – or Men in the Off Hours. Delights await!

Emily Wilson

Many congratulations to Anne Carson for the well-deserved Nobel prize! This is also great news for translation, classics, poetry, the breaking of generic and disciplinary boundaries, and the fact that you don’t have to fit a pre-existing mould to have a brilliant, successful career.

Ocean Vuong

To see the Nobel Committee honour a mind and spirit of such immense capacity and rigour gives me hope for the role of letters in our world at an hour when the vocation’s integrity is more threatened than ever before. For decades, Carson’s unapologetically erudite work has centered strangeness and mystery as methods of human revelation. And its myriad and restless formal enactments have granted endless permissions to multiple generations of writers. Like the best work out there, it fosters others as it forges new ways to be and think for itself. I count myself lucky to write in its wake.

Rebecca Perry

In 2013, I (and pretty much every writer I knew at the time) went to see Anne Carson give the Poetry Society annual lecture. She had us gripped, of course; she was generous, smart, sharp, impeccable in cowboy boots and a suit. Her person demands undivided attention. At the end, in the Q&A, a man asked a long, self-indulgent question to which she simply replied: “No.” The audience waited, briefly, for elaboration. None came.

And there lies the magic of Anne Carson – she is concurrently at play and utterly serious. She never gives many words when one will do.

For most of my writing life she has been the writer I go to for pretty much anything I need. I pick up The Beauty of the Husband and I fall in love with poetry again, I deal out the pamphlets of Float and remember that ambition and weirdness are good, I teach The Glass Essay and it shows up notions of formal boundaries as an absurdity.

She shows us that there is always, that there must be, room for risk and vision, for uncompromising writing. Poets everywhere are rejoicing.

entries.title: Agate Head / Stone Soup by Patricia Lockwood review – a gem of a collection
entries.summary: Inspired by stones and metals, the memoirist and novelist’s first poetry collection for more than a decade is charming, whimsical and intimateIn the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years, Patricia Lockwood states that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being pa
entries.content:
In the introduction to her first book of poetry in 12 years, Patricia Lockwood states that, “For almost a decade … I had not been able to hear it. The poems that I wrote would not end … too much was happening, there was a different kind of attention being paid.” It wasn’t that she didn’t want them to arrive. From Cave Painting: “And does she still write poems? / Not a whole one since I had been ill. / Five years. I kept saying I was / Doing it privately. So private even / I didn’t know about it.”

In that intervening period, Lockwood’s status has jumped from interesting US poet famous for the viral sensation Rape Joke to literary superstar: an acclaimed memoirist and novelist whose freewheeling, antic style is for many the internet’s maelstrom lassoed and put back on to the page. Who else can claim to have turned an audience with the pope into a biting comic essay?

So her return to poetry is a genuine event, and across Agate Head / Stone Soup there are countless moments that remind you that her poetic voice is unique: charming, whimsical, intimate; able to deliver images of great beauty, piercing philosophical insights and glimpses into a creative life behind the public persona. Readers of her memoir Priestdaddy will be pleased to see her father reappear in a few poems. “That my father has been drinking … / Always something new with him, / But I must say I didn’t see / 5-600 dollars’ worth of fine olive oil coming.”

Agate Head / Stone Soup is presented tête-bêche – head-to-tail in French, the volumes upside down and back-to-back. And while this might appear to be a frippery, the two collections have enough differences in texture to warrant it. Agate Head feels the more public-facing, while Stone Soup wrestles with more existential concerns, as beautifully rendered in Babies Born Remembering: “Screaming in the airport. / What do they remember – / Night flights, riding birds, / Being a set of wings / Themselves, a soul, an updraft.”

Both collections are inspired by stones, gems and metals of all shapes and sorts. Lockwood has been collecting fossils and minerals from an early age, and she and her husband have spent time learning metalsmithing, too. This gives her rich territories to explore. In Margaret De Patta, “Quartz wants / To be a window, wants a woman to appear. / We have properties, we are non-precious, / Wood horn bone and hair.” In An Agate a Day, we get to see her and her husband cutting agates, a hard stone with bands of different colours: “The trick is to hold the miracle steady. / We are the first to be seeing this. Ever. / Together. What happened to you? / We croon, after each cut.” It is notable that agates are associated with a sense of grounding and balance; an attempt to counteract all that other “attention”.

There is a detectable technical shift in Lockwood’s poems also. Many of the poems in 2014’s Motherland Fatherland Homelandsexuals featured long lines, allowed to run on and gather momentum to their epiphanies or punchlines. Here her lines are more staccato in feeling, jumpier in syntax, as in Not Seeing Glass Flowers: “To grow. Was it that / They looked real? I asked everyone. / Or was it something more? Max Beckmann’s painting is still a horror.”

It means a spikier initial impression for many of the poems. This ultimately works in their favour, as the thoughts accrete, moving in unlikely directions, before resolving into a revelation of some force. “Artists, no one really / Knows where they come from, / They fall a long way from the sky / And land zigzag” as Forged in Fire has it.

Neither collection is flawless. At one level, it is impossible to get away from the autobiographical detail, and so some of the poems become a form of higher gossip, our noses pressed up against the glass of fame. Sedarising, for example, comes across as smug rather than amusing.

And there are occasions when an object under discussion cannot bear the metaphorical weight being placed upon it. Polish Flint is an offender here: “The perfect ring I had married myself with / (Of Polish flint) was pried apart as I fell. / In slow motion, it seemed, surrounded / By tourists, with enough time to think / Of everything.”

But these are small bumps when time and again Lockwood leaves you with the distinct impression that she can magically make the profane into the profound, the holy into the hilarious, as she does to most brilliant effect in Monastery Icons: Windows into Heaven: “It’s sounding a little bit / Like you can order a whole husband / From this catalog, as long as his name is The Lord / And you are a PRAYING VIRGIN NIGHTLIGHT: / Just what we need in these challenging times.”

entries.title: Book of Lives by Margaret Atwood audiobook review – a dryly funny memoir
entries.summary: The Handmaid’s Tale author reflects on her loves, losses and literary achievements in a memoir that showcases her wisdom and witMargaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir
entries.content:
Margaret Atwood had to be persuaded to write a memoir. The thought of writing about herself initially seemed “dead boring. Who wants to read about someone sitting at a desk messing up blank sheets of paper?” Yet, she continues, time passed and the possibility of a memoir took on a “lurid phosphorescent glow. ‘Wasn’t there something appealing in the idea?’ my sinister alter ego whispered … I could thank my benefactors, reward my friends, trash my enemies and pay off scores long forgotten by everyone but me.”

Subtitled “A Memoir of Sorts”, Book of Lives is the Canadian author’s account of her loves, losses and literary achievements (she has written just over 50 books, including novels, short stories and poetry collections), and a fine showcase for her wisdom and wit. What little score-settling she includes is purely for the punchline. When a poet told Atwood in the early 1970s that she wrote like a man – he intended it as a compliment – she told him he forgot the punctuation. “What you meant was, ‘She writes. Like a man’.”

The book is read by the author, who is 86. Her narration is leisurely, gravelly, drily funny and unmistakeably Atwood. Though she admits she can’t recall much about her early books, she remembers enough about the important ones, most notably 1986’s The Handmaid’s Tale, her landmark novel set in a dystopian future. When she showed an early draft to the novelist Valerie Martin, Atwood said: “I think I’m gonna get into trouble.” Martin read it and told her: “I think you’re gonna make a lot of money.”

Available via Vintage Digital, 25hr 36min

Further listening

The Persian

David McCloskey, Swift Press Audio, 13hr 23min

This tense spy thriller from the CIA analyst turned author and podcaster sees Kamran, a Jewish Iranian dentist living in Sweden after being driven out of Iran, returning to his home country as a Mossad agent. Fajer Al-Kaisi is the narrator.

Elemental

Arthur Snell, Wildfire, 12hr 28min

Former diplomat Snell reads his compelling study of the huge geopolitical problems caused by the climate crisis – including mass migration, drought, rising sea levels and food and energy shortages – and how they can be addressed.

entries.title: Blockers by Michael Lewis review – the quiet heroes who tried to stop Doge
entries.summary: The author of Moneyball brings his exceptional narrative skills to bear on Musk’s anti-government crusadeDonald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American go
entries.content:
Donald Trump’s catastrophic errors get so much attention that his systemic ones can easily be missed. While the world looks on in dismay at his farcical war in Iran, the thuggery of Ice agents or clownish attacks on erstwhile allies like Canada and Denmark, the core functions of the American government are slowly disintegrating.

It is harder to get people to focus on the machinery of the state because the effects are often slow and hard to pin down. Outbreaks of disease – such as the recent wave of explosive diarrhoea across the US – might have happened anyway, but were probably made worse by lay-offs at the Centers for Disease Control. Likewise, Trump is not directly responsible for natural disasters, but response times in the past year may have been hampered by mass redundancies at the National Weather Service. Cuts to tax collection also seem to have reduced revenue by multiple billions, though we cannot be sure of the causal relationship.

The other problem is that bureaucracies are hard to make interesting. Their work is technical and complicated, and most officials are taught to avoid saying anything engaging in public. By the time a journalist has explained what an agency does and why it is important, the reader may well have clicked on to the next thing.

So there are few better suited to the challenge of telling this story than Michael Lewis, one of the world’s bestselling nonfiction writers, who has a knack for finding an angle that cuts through the complexity. After a career spent getting readers excited about credit default swaps (The Big Short) and sabermetrics (Moneyball) he has decided to try to help people understand the importance of civil servants.

Blockers is a loose sequel to the The Fifth Risk, in which Lewis focused on the transition from the Obama to the Trump administration and the disruption caused by the new team’s almost complete lack of interest in their jobs. It focused heavily on what different departments and agencies do and why they matter. This time around the problem is not indifference but malicious intent to destroy. The “blockers” are the dedicated officials who try to stop the wanton and often illegal destruction of their life’s work by Elon Musk’s Doge or other agents of chaos. They range from a researcher working on preventing wildfires to a security guard trying to block Musk’s goons from entering his building, and a lawyer attempting to keep personal tax data from being used to deport undocumented migrants.

In truth, they don’t do much blocking – since they all either end up resigning when they’re asked to do something illegal, or are fired. The title refers more to the assumption by Musk and his fellow travellers that these are the people who are stopping progress and need removing. Much of the book is taken up with descriptions of the valuable work they did before being turfed out.

It would have been good to have a bit more on the villains, whose motivations for participating in Doge are varied. They range from the addled young coders with limited social skills deployed by Musk, to turncoat bureaucrats looking for any easy life, and some very strange characters such as health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr, with his bizarre obsession with dead animal parts. Trump’s absurd commerce secretary Howard Lutnick also makes a brief cameo, deciding he needs to personally sign off any cheque for more than $100,000. It feels as if there is more to say about the personal journeys that lead people to behave this way.

This is the particularly true of the boss baddie Russell Vought, the Republican operative central to developing the Project 2025 plans for Trump’s second term. Musk causes havoc, but quickly gets bored of Doge and heads back to Silicon Valley. Vought is the real deal, quietly and systematically deconstructing the state while keeping out of the spotlight and getting others to do his dirty work for him.

He appears in one of the book’s most engaging chapters, which zooms in on Francis Collins, a scientist who helped discover a successful treatment for cystic fibrosis, allowing those with the condition to live much longer. Collins ended up at the head of the National Institutes of Health under Obama, continued through Trump’s first term and part of Biden’s, before stepping down to run an NIH research lab. After Trump’s re-election he was effectively forced out, saying that his position had become “untenable”. Lewis runs through a series of possible culprits, of which Vought’s cost-cutting is one. What makes this particularly remarkable is that Vought’s own daughter has cystic fibrosis. Ideology is a powerful drug.

But perhaps the most interesting character of all is Sahil Lavingia. A successful software engineer, he bought into Musk’s vision and went to work for Doge in the Department of Veterans Affairs. He only lasted 55 days before giving an on-the-record interview in which he noted that “it’s kind of fine – because the government works. It’s not as inefficient as I was expecting, to be honest. I was hoping for more easy wins.” This was not on-message and he was shown the door.

A few months later, though, once Doge had fallen apart, he was invited back by one of the few survivors, who had stayed on at the Treasury department. Lavingia was tasked with improving the Internal Revenue Service’s computer systems, and despite not needing the money, seems genuinely committed to the task of making things work better. Through Lavingia, Lewis gives us a taste of what serious work to enhance the state might have looked like.

There are real problems with the way the government operates, both in the UK and the US, caused by poor resourcing, dysfunctional systems, or low pay for technical staff compared with the private sector. Alongside Lewis’s star civil servants, there are people who have checked out or become institutionalised. Lavingia’s lengthy battle to get a water cooler replaced reminded me of how difficult it was to get the lifts working when I was at the Department for Education.

One of the most irritating aspects of Doge’s brief existence was the stream of op-eds from people who really should have known better celebrating that someone was finally trying to enact reform, even if was being done in a clumsy and aggressive manner. In reality, Musk’s overweening arrogance, glibness and total lack of preparation have seriously harmed the case for proper reform. Not just due to the mess he and the likes of Vought caused, but also because they brought the very idea of making the state more efficient into disrepute.

Lewis is great at finding incredible civil servants and telling their stories. But agencies and departments should not have to rely on unsung heroes, battling failing systems, and doing 90-hour weeks for little money because of their intense devotion to public service. Most people employed by large organisations are not like that. Effective government needs processes that work when used by a regular person doing a nine-to-five job. Rather than trying to replicate the “blockers”, we need to understand what these superstars are doing and embed it in the fabric of our institutions.

entries.title: Anne Carson and Can Xue favourites to win Nobel prize in literature
entries.summary: The Canadian poet and Chinese experimental writer are the bookmakers’ favourites to win, with Haruki Murakami, Gerald Murnane and Margaret Atwood also in the mixCanadian poet Anne Carson and Chinese experimental writer Can Xue are the bookies’ favourites to win this year’s Nobel prize in literature, set to be announced Thursday.The frontrunners both have 10/1 odds of taking home the world’s most p
entries.content:
Canadian poet Anne Carson and Chinese experimental writer Can Xue are the bookies’ favourites to win this year’s Nobel prize in literature, set to be announced Thursday.

The frontrunners both have 10/1 odds of taking home the world’s most prestigious literary prize, this year worth 12m Swedish Krona (approximately £900,000), according to Ladbrokes.

The 76-year-old Carson is known for her hybrid style, mixing poetry and prose, and combining contemporary stories with ancient myth. Among her best-known works is her 1998 verse novel Autobiography of Red, a queer coming-of-age story that reworks a Greek poem about Heracles.

Can Xue has been a favourite for several years running. The 73-year-old, whose real name is Deng Xiaohua, has twice been longlisted for the International Booker for the novel Love in the New Millennium – translated by Annelise Finegan Wasmoen – and for her short story collection I Live in the Slums, translated by Karen Gernant and Chen Zeping.

Coming in behind Carson and Can Xue is Haruki Murakami with odds of 14/1. The Japanese writer is one of the biggest international sellers among the favourites, known for works including Norwegian Wood and Kafka on the Shore.

Ladbrokes also have Australian avant garde writer Gerald Murnane in the mix, along with American postmodern novelist Thomas Pynchon, both with odds of 16/1.

And at 20/1 odds are seven writers: Margaret Atwood, Cristina Rivera Garza, Enrique Vila-Matas, Jamaica Kincaid, Lídia Jorge, Lyudmila Ulitskaya and Michel Houellebecq.

Canadian novelist Atwood, author of The Handmaid’s Tale, already has many of literature’s biggest prizes under her belt, including the Booker and the Giller prize.

Meanwhile, Mexican author Rivera Garza won the Pulitzer prize in 2024 for Liliana’s Invincible Summer, a memoir about her 20-year-old sister, who was murdered by a former boyfriend.

Vila-Matas is one of Spain’s most prominent novelists, known for blending fiction with essay. In 2020, he was longlisted for the International Booker prize for his metafictional novel Mac and His Problem, translated by Margaret Jull Costa and Sophie Hughes.

Kincaid is an Antiguan-American writer, best known for books including Annie John, A Small Place and Lucy, which often explore family relationships and colonialism’s destructiveness. Kincaid “is a writer you don’t just read; she is a writer that takes you back to yourself”, wrote the poet Jackie Kay in 2022.

At longer odds are Karl Ove Knausgård, Alexis Wright, Colm Tóibín, César Aira, Deborah Levy, Don DeLillo, Emmanuel Carrère, Leila Aboulela, Michael Ondaatje, Mircea Cărtărescu and Salman Rushdie.

The winner will be announced at 12pm UK time (1pm CEST) on Thursday. Last year’s recipient was the Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai. Other recent winners include Han Kang, Jon Fosse, Annie Ernaux and Abdulrazak Gurnah.

entries.title: Other Worlds Than These by Stephen King and Peter Straub review – a self-indulgent finale to the Talisman trilogy
entries.summary: There are moments of shivering joy as the protagonist of two enduring classics, Jack Sawyer, returns – but this time his journey feels endlessly repetitiveBear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stori
entries.content:
Bear with me, because there is some backstory to get through before we can talk about the book I am actually here to review. Back in 1984, Stephen King and Peter Straub collaborated on the fantasy novel The Talisman. Like all the best King stories, it follows a young boy: in this case Jack Sawyer, 12, whose mother, Lily, is dying. Jack learns that a magical object called the Talisman might save her – if he can find it in a parallel world known as the Territories. Straub and King followed this up in 2001 with Black House, in which an adult Jack investigates a series of child murders that turn out to have disturbing links to the Territories.

The books are very different: one a coming-of-age cross-country quest, in which Jack flips back and forth between two versions of the US; the other a fantastical and horror-inflected murder mystery. Both are brilliant and enduring classics which will always have a place on my bookshelves – I reread both of them, all 1,800-odd pages, to prepare for Other Worlds Than These and was as swept away and delighted as the first time round.

So: in 2013 Straub had an idea for a final volume in the Talisman trilogy, drawing as Black House does from a real-life series of murders, and returning Jack (previously left on a bit of a cliffhanger) to the fray. King didn’t pick up on it back then, and Straub died in 2022. Now King is 79, and, as he writes in a somewhat valedictory afterword, “it’s time to think about tidying up, as much as such things are possible for a writer whose mind is still crammed with cool ideas”. So he went back to that old idea – the original email lost, but the concept of a “series of motiveless, brutal crimes” in the Far West of the Territories, as Straub put it, at the story’s heart.

Jack, “his tide … going out”, is now 57. An aimless, lonely émigré to the Territories, he is sent on a mission by the two-bit despot he now depressingly reports to. He’s to travel through the toxic Blasted Lands to gather information on the Great Gorge, a mysterious area of “growing danger” that Governor Youngblood wants to know more about. Flipping back and forth between “America-side” and the Territories, Jack learns that an old policeman friend has gone missing on the trail of a pair of “murderin’ kids” who have been leaving a swathe of bodies in their wake in Nebraska. These kids are, he’s told, “infested” by demons – and the infestation is spreading to the children of the Territories.

For the true King fan (the “Constant Reader”, as he puts it), there are moments of shivering joy in Other Worlds Than These – not least in the title, which draws from a key scene in King’s The Gunslinger. I could never not find pleasure in a billy-bumbler (a dog-like creature), or in memories of Wolf, a wonderful creation from The Talisman, or in references to chief gunslinger Roland Deschain from the Dark Tower series. As befits King, there are moments of true horror too, and good ones, as the teenage infection spreads across the Territories.

But I cannot recommend that anyone who is not a Constant Reader embark on this 800-plus-page tome. For one, it would be pointless to read it without previously having read The Talisman and Black House (and if I’m honest, probably the seven-volume Dark Tower sequence too). And even for the Constant Reader, this is really not vintage King. I would have said that I’d follow Jack Sawyer anywhere, but as Ole Travellin’ Jack crisscrossed his way across the dry desert land of the Territories, his journey started to feel endless, and endlessly repetitive. As Jack’s crew are gearing up to cross yet another rickety bridge over yet another gaping chasm, one character even makes this point when they spot it. “Oh God … talk about repetition.” I hear you, fella! Jack himself does it: “Another echo. They’re becoming tiresome,” he says, in a rather too on-the-nose comment about the eerie (not so eerie the nth time they’re mentioned) similarities between the US and the Territories.

Is this deliberate? Yes, undoubtedly: “ka [destiny] is a wheel”, as we’ve been told (more than once); Jack, as Roland did before him, is treading the path laid out for him in an endless cycle. But this time round, it all gets a little portentous, self-referential and self-indulgent – and, dare I say it, boring.

I still think Stephen King is a genius. I still think The Talisman is the perfect coming-of-age dark fantasy novel. So thank you for the endless hours of reading pleasure, Mr King. But unlike its predecessors, Other Worlds Than These will not be going on my reread shelf.

entries.title: Partita By Barbara Kingsolver review – a midlife follow-up to Demon Copperhead
entries.summary: The sex writing threatens to throw the novel off-kilter, but there are rich rewards in this tale of music and middle-aged compromisesWhat is the role of art in an artist’s life? Should you commit everything to honing your talent in the hope of becoming a great master? Or should you use your artistic gift to enrich your life and that of your community? In Partita, acclaimed American novelist Barbar
entries.content:
What is the role of art in an artist’s life? Should you commit everything to honing your talent in the hope of becoming a great master? Or should you use your artistic gift to enrich your life and that of your community? In Partita, acclaimed American novelist Barbara Kingsolver grapples with these questions seriously and passionately through the story of a piano prodigy turned music teacher.

The novel opens in the present, where Livia is a school music teacher in the same part of rural Tennessee where she grew up, married to a farmer who once worked on her father’s farm. Contented middle age has been disturbed by a phone call from Sigurd, a man she had an all-consuming, destructive love affair with at college. This pulls her back into her past: both the period of her brother’s suicide when she was 11, and the years when she escaped on a music scholarship to Indiana, convinced she was leaving her parents’ world behind for good. We discover that her dreams of being a world-class pianist were shattered by an accident that damaged her hand, and that Sigurd played a part in this.

The two timeframes present two visions of the role of music in a life, and two visions of love as well. Livia in the present seems content to be the inspirational local music teacher that she herself had to go much further to find, but it’s clear that the 20-year-old Livia would have considered such a life a failure, and that her faith in her own talent was justified. Livia now is happy with sex as comfort – “like putting a heating pad on an aching muscle”. Yet she still relies on memories of another kind of sex to reach orgasm – sex with Sigurd that she remembers as comprising the tension and release of music: “harmonic tension, dynamic tension, oh my dear lord, the rubato, his movements slowing, slowing, robbing me of the truth of the beat until I begged for justice … Sometimes we both shed tears.”

It’s unfair to quote sex writing out of context, and I feel bad doing it here, but this breathless, overwrought prose runs through the account of Livia’s affair with Sigurd, threatening to throw the whole novel off-kilter. We know from Kingsolver’s other novels how assured her writing usually is, so the gaucheness felt out of place. But Kingsolver commits to her protagonists’ language more fervently than most novelists and I ended up deciding that this must be what’s happening here. There’s no doubt in Demon Copperhead that the brash vernacular is Demon’s own, because the voice is closer to speech than to writing. Here, Livia’s voice is more literary, and so harder to distinguish from Kingsolver’s. But sentences such as “this wasn’t proper by a long shot: fingers craving to know the sandpaper of his jaw” are surely Livia’s, and the florid prose is a sign that she’s carried away by memories of the erotic apex of her life.

Indeed, it’s revealing that Livia’s voice is subtler when it comes to music, which has seen her through into middle age while lust’s flame has faded. Kingsolver – who herself went to college with a music scholarship to study classical piano – is clearly fascinated by music, and how to write about it, and her gifts seem to entwine with Livia’s in the descriptions of piano pieces. Injured and learning to play again, Livia tries Chopin’s B minor Prelude, slowly and tentatively, and finds her own sadness reflected and transformed. “The sadness is all in the melody line the left hand keeps bringing up from below, a slow arpeggio trying to climb up out of the dark, but after a few notes of rising, it falls back down … It’s the God’s honest truth of grief. It doesn’t resolve.”

Livia’s discovery here is huge; she’s coming to understand that a piece of music can enrich the performer and her audience even when the performance might be judged second-rate. Kingsolver is a committed social novelist – she’s even set up a prize to honour the socially engaged novel – and, ultimately, Partita is an impassioned testament to the need for art in ordinary communities, and the need for ordinariness in art. This means, in turn, that these communities have to put aside their own suspicions about artistic elitism, honouring the talents of artists in their midst by sending them away to study if necessary.

Livia says early on that when you have a gift, “it feels like there’s a rule that you have to keep doing it. Not just that you owe it to yourself, you owe it to the world. Maybe to God. As payback on the borrowed gift.” She manages to sustain this vision, even as what it means to “keep doing it” changes for her. Her sister-in-law – herself a gifted scholar of literature, now happy to teach English – helps her to see that “the point of art is to help you like your life better” and that this can mean being a local piano teacher rather than an international soloist. “This was all I needed, back then,” Livia thinks sadly, “Somebody to tell me this.”

Partita doesn’t offer the immediate satisfactions of Demon Copperhead; it’s a quieter book, slower to get going and to make its world enticing. But it’s a rich novel and one that I’ve found has opened up a dialogue with me as a reader that’s continued long after I finished reading it. Kingsolver doesn’t make light of what Livia has lost, and so she’s all the more convincing in her insistence that there’s as much to be gained in the compromises of middle age, and that artists may be following their calling most fully when they find ways to make their art part of a vibrant, loving collective life within our communities.
